why_correct: A State has four essential elements: population, territory, government and sovereignty. Religion is not among them, and a State may have any religion or none, as a secular State does.

why_wrong.0: Population is essential; there can be no State without people.
why_wrong.1: Government is essential, being the machinery through which the State acts.
why_wrong.2: Sovereignty is essential, and it is what distinguishes a State from any other association. Territory is the fourth, and it is the one missing from this list of options.

why_correct: Pluralists hold that sovereignty is not the monopoly of the State but is shared among the many associations to which people belong: churches, trade unions, universities and local bodies. Laski and MacIver argued this against the monistic view.

why_wrong.0: Absolute and indivisible sovereignty is the monistic theory of Bodin, Hobbes and Austin, which pluralism was framed to attack.
why_wrong.2: Sovereignty held only by the monarch is the doctrine of divine right and absolute monarchy.
why_wrong.3: Sovereignty exercised only by the judiciary describes no theory, and would make the courts supreme over the legislature.

why_correct: Thomas Hobbes is most closely associated with the State of Nature, which he described in Leviathan as a war of every man against every man, where life was solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short.

why_wrong.0: Karl Marx explained the State as an instrument of class domination and predicted its withering away.
why_wrong.2: J. S. Mill wrote on liberty and representative government, not on a pre-political condition.
why_wrong.3: T. H. Green was an idealist who saw the State as removing obstacles to the good life. Locke and Rousseau also used the term, but of the four names offered only Hobbes belongs to that tradition.

why_correct: Individualists describe the State as a necessary evil. They hold that its interference restricts liberty, so it is an evil, but that it is needed to maintain order and protect rights, so it is necessary.

why_wrong.1: Idealists such as Hegel and Green regard the State as a positive good and even as the march of God on earth.
why_wrong.2: Socialists want the State to do more, not less, in order to secure economic equality.
why_wrong.3: Fascists glorify the State absolutely, holding that the individual exists for it.

why_correct: The Social Contract Theory explains the State as arising from an agreement among people who left the state of nature to secure order. Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau each gave their own version of it.

why_wrong.0: The Force Theory holds that the State arose from conquest by the strong.
why_wrong.1: The Divine Origin Theory holds that the State was created by God and the ruler is His representative.
why_wrong.3: The Evolutionary Theory holds that the State grew gradually from the family, without any single founding act.

why_correct: Rousseau located sovereignty in the General Will, the will of the community aiming at the common good. It is not the mere sum of individual wills but what all would will as citizens.

why_wrong.0: Hobbes placed sovereignty in an absolute ruler to whom people surrendered all rights.
why_wrong.1: Locke placed ultimate authority with the people but expressed it through a limited government and the right of resistance, not through a general will.
why_wrong.3: Austin placed sovereignty in a determinate human superior whose commands are habitually obeyed.

why_correct: John Austin gave the legal or monistic theory of sovereignty, defining the sovereign as a determinate human superior who receives habitual obedience and owes it to no one else. Law, for him, is the sovereign's command.

why_wrong.0: Harold Laski was the leading pluralist and a critic of exactly this theory.
why_wrong.1: J. A. Hobson wrote on imperialism and economics.
why_wrong.3: MacIver was a sociologist who also criticised the monistic view and distinguished the State from society.

why_correct: The external aspect of sovereignty is independence from foreign control, meaning the State is free to conduct its own affairs and is not subject to any other State.

why_wrong.0: Law-making power is internal, exercised over the State's own people and territory.
why_wrong.1: Taxation is likewise an internal power.
why_wrong.3: Judicial authority is internal too. The division is simply direction: inward over its own subjects, outward against other States.

why_correct: The Force Theory holds that the State originated in conquest, the strong subduing the weak and imposing their rule. War, said the theory's critics, made the king and the king made war.

why_wrong.0: Origin from the family is the Evolutionary or Patriarchal theory.
why_wrong.1: Creation by divine command is the Divine Origin Theory.
why_wrong.3: Gradual evolution is again the Evolutionary Theory, which is the modern and most accepted explanation.

why_correct: Sir Henry Maine is the chief exponent of the Evolutionary Theory, tracing the growth of the State from family to gens, tribe and finally State, and describing the movement from status to contract.

why_wrong.1: Rousseau is a social contract theorist.
why_wrong.2: Austin gave the legal theory of sovereignty, not an account of the State's origin.
why_wrong.3: Bodin first systematised the concept of sovereignty in the sixteenth century.

why_correct: Locke supported limited government. He held that people surrender only some rights, that the government is a trustee bound by natural law, and that people may resist it if it breaks the trust.

why_wrong.0: Hobbes argued for an absolute sovereign, since only unlimited power could prevent a return to the war of all against all.
why_wrong.2: Mussolini founded fascism, which subordinates the individual entirely to the State.
why_wrong.3: Austin's sovereign is legally unlimited and subject to no restraint. Hobbes and Locke are the pair to keep straight: both use the contract, but reach opposite conclusions about how much power the ruler should have.

why_correct: Popular sovereignty means that ultimate authority rests with the people, from whom all governmental power is derived. The Indian Constitution opens with We, the people of India, on that principle.

why_wrong.0: Sovereignty in the king is monarchical sovereignty, defended by the divine right theory.
why_wrong.2: Sovereignty in Parliament alone is legal sovereignty, as in the British doctrine. Popular sovereignty lies behind it, since Parliament is elected.
why_wrong.3: Sovereignty in the military describes a dictatorship, which is the negation of the idea.

why_correct: The Divine Origin Theory rests on faith rather than evidence. It cannot be tested historically, and it was largely abandoned once the Reformation, the rise of science and democratic ideas undermined it.

why_wrong.0: The Evolutionary Theory is supported by anthropological and historical evidence of tribal societies developing into States.
why_wrong.1: The Force Theory has considerable historical support, since many States were indeed founded by conquest.
why_wrong.3: The Social Contract Theory is criticised as unhistorical, which makes it a fair guess, but it is at least argued from reason rather than from faith.

why_correct: Hegel regarded the State as an ethical institution, the highest expression of the moral idea, in which the individual realises true freedom. His idealism was later developed by T. H. Green and Bosanquet.

why_wrong.1: Locke saw the State as a limited trustee for protecting life, liberty and property.
why_wrong.2: Bentham was a utilitarian and judged the State by whether it produced the greatest happiness of the greatest number.
why_wrong.3: Laski was a pluralist who denied the State any such moral supremacy over other associations.

why_correct: Political sovereignty in a democracy rests with the electorate, the body of voters behind the legal sovereign. Their verdict at elections is the power that legal authority must ultimately answer to.

why_wrong.1: The army is subordinate to civilian authority in a democracy.
why_wrong.2: The bureaucracy executes policy but does not make or legitimise it.
why_wrong.3: The judiciary interprets the law. Legal sovereignty lies with the law-making body and political sovereignty behind it with the voters, and that pairing is what the question tests.

why_correct: Sovereignty is inalienable, meaning it cannot be given away, and territory is not one of its characteristics at all. Transferability of territory is therefore not a feature of sovereignty.

why_wrong.0: Permanence is a genuine feature: sovereignty lasts as long as the State does, whoever governs.
why_wrong.1: Absoluteness is a feature in the monistic theory, meaning the sovereign is subject to no higher legal power.
why_wrong.2: Universality within the territory is a feature, since sovereignty extends over every person and association inside the State. Alongside these go indivisibility, inalienability and exclusiveness.

why_correct: Locke wrote to justify constitutional, limited government, and his Two Treatises defended the English Glorious Revolution of 1688. His ideas later shaped the American Declaration of Independence.

why_wrong.0: Absolute monarchy is what Hobbes's version of the contract justified, and what Locke was arguing against.
why_wrong.2: Military rule finds no support anywhere in Locke.
why_wrong.3: Theocracy is government by religious authority, which Locke opposed in his Letter Concerning Toleration.

why_correct: Aristotle defined the State in his Politics as a union of families and villages having for its end a perfect and self-sufficing life. He held that the State comes into being for life and continues for the good life.

why_wrong.1: Plato described an ideal state in The Republic built on justice and the division of classes, but this definition is Aristotle's.
why_wrong.2: Rousseau wrote of the general will and the social contract.
why_wrong.3: T. H. Green defined the State as removing hindrances to the good life, which is a related idea from a much later idealist.

why_correct: The Divine Origin Theory supported absolute monarchy, since a king who ruled by God's will was answerable to God alone and could not be resisted or judged by his subjects.

why_wrong.0: Democracy rests on popular sovereignty, which is the opposite claim.
why_wrong.1: Constitutionalism means limited government under law, which divine right rejects.
why_wrong.3: Socialism concerns economic organisation and arose centuries later. James I of England and Louis XIV of France are the standard examples of rulers who invoked the theory.

why_correct: Commercial sovereignty is not a recognised form. The forms discussed in political science are legal, political, popular, de jure, de facto and titular sovereignty.

why_wrong.0: Legal sovereignty is the authority recognised by law to issue commands.
why_wrong.1: Political sovereignty is the power behind the legal sovereign, in modern States the electorate.
why_wrong.2: Popular sovereignty is the doctrine that ultimate authority rests with the people. Trade and commerce are regulated by a sovereign State, but they are not a kind of sovereignty.

why_correct: Austin held that in every political society there is a determinate human superior who receives habitual obedience from the bulk of the people and renders obedience to no one. That obedience is the mark of sovereignty.

why_wrong.1: People's participation belongs to popular sovereignty, and Austin's theory is legal rather than democratic.
why_wrong.2: Group autonomy is the pluralist position, framed in opposition to Austin.
why_wrong.3: International cooperation limits sovereignty in practice, and Austin's theory makes no room for it. His three key terms are determinate, habitual obedience and legally unlimited.

why_correct: The chief criticism of Hobbes is that his contract justifies absolute authority. People surrender all their rights irrevocably to a sovereign who is party to no agreement, leaving them no right of resistance however tyrannical he becomes.

why_wrong.0: Hobbes does not promote democracy. He preferred monarchy as the most effective form of absolute rule.
why_wrong.2: He does not oppose sovereignty; he makes it unlimited.
why_wrong.3: Pluralism is the opposite of his position, which concentrates all authority in one sovereign.

why_correct: Harold Laski was the strongest critic of the monistic theory. He argued that the State is only one association among many and has no moral right to unlimited obedience, and that in reality power is federal and divided.

why_wrong.0: Bodin founded the monistic theory in the sixteenth century.
why_wrong.1: Austin gave it its classic legal statement.
why_wrong.3: Hobbes gave it its philosophical defence. The other three built the theory; Laski attacked it.

why_correct: The evolutionary explanation holds that the State grew gradually out of the family, kinship, religion, war and political consciousness working together over long ages. It is the explanation historians and anthropologists accept.

why_wrong.0: Creation in a single event describes the social contract theory, and evolution denies any such founding moment.
why_wrong.2: Foundation by God is the divine origin theory.
why_wrong.3: Military conquest alone is the force theory. Force did play a part in evolution, but as one factor among several rather than the whole explanation.

why_correct: Jean Bodin first gave a systematic account of sovereignty in his Six Books of the Commonwealth in 1576, defining it as supreme power over citizens and subjects, unrestrained by law.

why_wrong.1: Aristotle wrote on the State and its forms but had no developed concept of sovereignty, which is a modern idea tied to the nation-state.
why_wrong.2: Marx analysed the State in class terms in the nineteenth century.
why_wrong.3: T. H. Green was a nineteenth-century idealist. The sequence to remember runs Bodin, then Hobbes, then Austin.
